# University of Edinburgh
The University of Edinburgh, established in 1583 as Tounis College, is one of Scotland's most historic and prestigious institutions. It has a rich tradition of academic excellence and scientific innovation, having contributed significantly to fields such as antiseptic surgery (Joseph Lister), economics (Adam Smith), electromagnetism (James Clerk Maxwell), evolution (Charles Darwin), and many others. The university comprises multiple campuses within Edinburgh, including the Central Area (arts, humanities, social sciences, informatics), King's Buildings (science and engineering), BioQuarter (medical facilities and research), Easter Bush (veterinary studies and animal sciences), and Western General (biomedical research). Significant buildings include St Cecilia's Hall, Teviot Row House (world’s oldest purpose-built student union), and McEwan Hall (graduation venue).
Governance is based on the Universities (Scotland) Acts, with three main bodies: the University Court (governing body), General Council (graduates and staff), and Senatus Academicus (academic authority). The university is divided into three colleges—Arts, Humanities and Social Sciences; Science and Engineering; Medicine and Veterinary Medicine—housing 21 schools offering a broad range of degree programmes. Edinburgh medical and veterinary schools have historically been world-leading and maintain high rankings. The university is a member of the Russell Group and numerous international research alliances. It maintains a strong commitment to research, with income exceeding £1.3 billion annually and holding one of the largest endowments in the UK.
Student life is vibrant, with over 250 societies led by the Edinburgh University Students' Association, one of the oldest unions in the world. Sporting traditions include the Scottish Varsity rugby match and the Scottish Boat Race, with Edinburgh athletes excelling at the Olympics. The university experiences active student activism, including recent protests over ethical investment and international issues. Its historical and contemporary alumni include major figures in sciences, politics, arts, and beyond, contributing to its global reputation.
